We introduce FrontierCS, a benchmark of 156 open-ended problems across diverse areas of computer science, designed and reviewed by experts, including CS PhDs and top-tier competitive programming participants and problem setters.
FrontierCS targets problems where the optimal solution is unknown, but the quality of a solution can be objectively evaluated.
Models solve these tasks by implementing executable programs rather than outputting a direct answer.
For each problem we provide an expert reference solution and an automatic evaluator.
we find that frontier reasoning models still lag far behind human experts on both the algorithmic and research tracks
models often over-optimize for generating merely workable code instead of discovering high-quality algorithms and system designs.
the human achieves 87% density while GPT-5 achieves only 47%
Yet many frontier problems in computer science are intrinsically open-ended, requiring nuanced trade-offs among quality, efficiency, and robustness

We focus on tasks where a global optimum is either unknown or practically unattainable, yet any proposed solution can be deterministically checked for validity and assigned a score by an automatic evaluator
This design measures the ability of models to implement effective and efficient algorithms rather than algorithms that exhaustively solve the problem.

Left: Algorithmic Problems, covering Optimization tasks, Constructive tasks, and Interactive tasks, adapted from programming contests but rewritten into open-ended, partially scored variants. Right: Research Problems, spanning six major CS domains: OS (Operating Systems), HPC (High-Performance Computing), AI (Artificial Intelligence research tasks), DB (Databases), PL (Programming Languages), and Security (cybersecurity and vulnerability analysis). These research problems are sourced from real research workflows and each comes with a deterministic evaluator.
FrontierCS consists 156 problems across two tracks: Algorithmic Problems and Research Problems.
The Algorithmic Problems track contains 107 problems adapted from programming contests, covering three categories: Optimization, Constructive, and Interactive problems.
The Research Problems track contains 49 problems sourced from real-world computer science research questions, spanning six domains
we introduce a structured curation pipeline, i.e., Proposal, Implementation, and Review, to construct genuinely variants.

This stage is led by experts with qualifications equivalent to ICPC World Finalists, who are responsible for submitting candidate problems, complete with links to their original sources and a description of intended modifications.
FrontierCS contains 107 high-quality algorithmic problems adapted from programming contests, including 29 optimization problems, 27 constructive problems and 51 interactive problems.
Unless explicitly specified otherwise, runtime is never part of the scoring
measured relative to a trivial baseline and a strong human reference
In total, FrontierCS contains 49 research problems across diverse domains such as symbolic regression, vector database design, and kernel optimization.
the problem must support automated scoring via evaluate.sh, which gives a standardized score between 0 and 100
deterministic and must not use an LLM as a judge
we treat every variant as an independent problem in the reported totals
For FrontierCS research problems, we ask CS PhD students to set problems based on their unsolved research questions and to implement the evaluation container.
our evaluators provide a score of 0 – 100 using human performance as the baseline, allowing for measurable feedback on incremental improvements.
FrontierCS is designed to remain relevant as models improve by supporting three complementary forms of task evolution.
A key feature of FrontierCS is the separation between the written problem description and the environment in which the task is instantiated.

In our evaluation, we tested 9 frontier models: GPT 5 Thinking [40], Gemini 2.5 Pro [13], Gemini 3.0 Pro [14], Grok 4 [48], Claude Opus 4.1 [2], Claude Sonnet 4.5 [4], Claude Opus 4.5 [3], DeepSeek V3.2 Thinking [15].
We set time-out for each LLM request as 20 minutes.
models are tested in a single-round setting: once they produce a solution, that output is final.
They do not have the opportunity to run their code, inspect unit-test results, or iterate based on feedback.
They also do not have access to a code editor, a Python environment, or any external tools.
We leave the evaluation of multi-round, agentic, tool-call-assisted, and evolve-style frameworks to future work.
we introduce a grading system that scores each solution relative to two reference points: the reference solution written by human experts and a trivial baseline solution.
We report both Score@1, Avg@5, and Score@5, as we observe that the model exhibits stochasticity and notable improvement across multiple attempts.
we define Score@k as the maximum score among the k model trials, and Avg@k as the average score among those trials.
We also report Pass@1 and Pass@5: the fraction of problems where the model achieves a non-zero score, i.e., produces a valid solution that exceeds the the most trivial baseline.
In all evaluations, we do not use any agentic framework and require the model to directly output code.

As shown in Table 1, frontier models still lag significantly behind human experts on the algorithmic problems track, where the 8 frontier models achieve Score@1 of 10.87 (GPT 5 Thinking), 11.80 (GPT 5.1 Thinking), 12.53 (Gemini 2.5 Pro), 29.37 (Gemini 3.0 Pro), 13.67 (Grok 4), 14.95 (Claude Opus 4.5), 6.91 (Claude Opus 4.1), and 5.84 (Claude sonnet 4.5) respectively, compared to human experts’ 95.41.
Claude Opus 4.5 attains the best one-shot results (Score@1 29.40), while GPT 5.1 Thinking leads under multi-sample evaluation (Score@5 47.21).
increasing the reasoning effort from medium to high does not yield further gains; in fact, performance drops from 15.336 to 12.626
the model often fixates on small, low-impact optimizations while overlooking the core algorithmic choices required for substantial performance gains
FrontierCS provides expert reference solutions, an automated evaluator, and a fully reproducible pipeline, and adopts versioned difficulty scheduling to preserve discrimination as models improve.
competence on closed-form coding tasks does not reliably translate into open-ended problem solving.
Frontier-CS is an unsolved, open-ended, verifiable, and diverse benchmark for evaluating AI on challenging computer science problems.

FrontierCS 2: A Benchmark for Computer Science R&D
https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29932
FrontierCS 2 evaluates AI agents on their ability to do CS research. Each task removes the key contribution of a paper from the code released with it.
We delete a paper’s contribution from its own repository. The agent writes it back and is scored against the human reference, the code released with the paper.
It sees its repository and, for each patch it submits, a score on the development workloads and one message.
The hidden evaluation adds workloads the agent never sees, and the evaluator, the hidden workloads and the reference stay with the judge.
A run passes only when its final submission beats the human reference on every metric the task checks and on every hidden workload.
A higher total score is not enough: a run that is faster on average but worse on one metric or one workload does not pass.
The final score averages over every metric and every hidden workload, so a large gain in one place can hide a loss in another.
An agent may end on a version that fails although an earlier one would have passed.
We want agents to push the research frontier, with a result the paper’s authors would accept as better.
Each run has a wall-clock budget of 5 hours.
Each task’s evaluator also scores the final submission on the hidden suite, from 0 to 100, and a run that ends without a final submission scores 0.
The mean score chart averages each run’s score minus the human reference’s score on the same task, so 0 means level with the human reference.
FCI, the FrontierCS Capabilities Index, applies the idea of Epoch AI’s ECI to what decides a pass.
The human reference has no FCI, since its code cannot pass against itself.
Choosing which version to submit is part of the work we measure, so we do not correct the choice
The 48 tasks, their evaluators and the judge are public as one evaluation environment at github.com/FrontierCS/FrontierCS-2.
It installs into your own AWS account.
The results cover 960 runs on 48 tasks by 20 models.
Kimi K2.7 is fixed at 5; its runs take part in the fit, but it is not on the leaderboard.
For Claude Opus 5.5, one full evaluation of the 48 tasks costs about US$1,000 in API fees, US$300 in GPU time and US$100 in CPU time.
Pass rate by domain
Gemini 4 Argon (Antigravity): refused requests are retried. In Structured LWE the retries ran out and the run ended, and in CREST refused context summaries were kept cut short.
The hardest task sits at FDI 102.2, above every model, so the scale does not saturate the way a pass rate does.
A task’s FDI is the FCI a model needs to pass it half the time, so a model’s FCI says which tasks it can be expected to pass.

FCI is a fork of Epoch AI’s Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI), fitted on what decides a pass, each metric’s beat or miss against the human reference, and on how far each final score lands from it, instead of raw scores
The private set has more than 100 tasks and will be announced in the future.
